title: Bartholmew fayre : a comedie, acted in the yeare, 1614 by the Lady Elizabeths seruants, and then dedicated to King Iames, of most blessed memorie ; The diuell is an asse : a comedie acted in the yeare, 1616, by His Maiesties seruants ; The staple of newes : a comedie acted in the yeare, 1625, by His Maiesties seruants by the author, Beniamin Iohnson.
author: Jonson, Ben, 1573?-1637.

plays.play_title: The first Intermeane after the first Act.

segments.head: The first Intermeane after the first Act.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: How now Gossip! how doe's the Play please you?

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: Very scuruily, me thinks, and sufficiently naught.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: As a body would wish: here's nothing but a young Prodigall, come of age, who makes much of the Barber, buyes him a place in a new Office, i'the ayre, I know not where, and his man o'Law to follow him, with the Begger to boote, and they two helpe him to a wife.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: I, shee is a proper piece! that such creatures can broke for.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: I cannot abide that nasty fellow, the Begger, if hee had beene a Court-Begger in good clothes; a Begger in veluet, as they say, I could haue endur'd him.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: Or a begging scholler in blacke, or one of these beggerly Poets, gossip, that would hang vpon a young heyre like a horseleech.

speeches.speaker: EXPEC.
prose: Or a thred-bare Doctor of Physicke, a poore Quackesaluer.

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: Or a Sea-captaine, halfe steru'd.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: I, these were tolerable Beggers, Beggers of fashion! you shall see some such anon!

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: I would faine see the Foole, gossip, the Foole is the finest man t'the company, they say, and has all the wit: Hee is the very Iustice o' Peace o'the Play, and can cemmit whom hee will, and what hee will, errour, absurdity, as the toy takes him, and no man say, blacke is his eye, but laugh at him.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: But they ha' no Foole i' this Play, I am afraid, gossip.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: It's a wise Play, then.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: They are all fooles, the rather, in that.

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: Like enough.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: My husband, (Timothy Tatle, God rest his poore soule) was wont to say, there was no Play without a Foole, and a Diuell in't; he was for the Diuell still God blesse him. The Diuell for his money, would hee say, I would faine see the Diuell. And why would you so faine see the Diuell? would I say. Because hee has hornes, wife, and may be a cuckold, as well as a Diuell, hee would answer: You are e'en such another, husband, quoth I. Was the Diuell euer married? where doe you read, the Di^ll was euer so honorable to commit Matrimony; The Play will tell vs, that, sayes hee, wee'll goe see't to morrow, the Diuell is an Asse. Hee is an errant learn'd man, that made it, and can write, they say, and I am fouly deceiu'd, but hee can read too.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: I remember it gossip, I went with you, by the same token, Mrs. Trouble Truth diswaded vs, and told vs, hee was a prophane Poet, and all his Playes had Diuels in them. That he kept schole vpo' the Stage, could coniure there, aboue the Schole of Westminster, and Doctor Lamb too: not a Play he made, but had a Diuell in it. And that he would learne vs all to make our husbands Cuckolds at Playes: by another token, that a young married wife i'the company, said, shee could finde in her heart to steale thither, and see a little o'the vanity through her masque, and come practice at home.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: O, it was, Mistresse—

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: Nay, Gossip, I name no body. It may be 'twas my selfe.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: But was the Diuell a proper man, Gossip?

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose:
As fine a gentleman. of his inches, as euer I saw trusted to the Stage
. or any where else: and lou'd the common wealth, as well as ere a Patriot of 'hem all: hee would carry away the Vice on his backe, quicke to Hell, in euery Play where he came, and reforme abuses.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: There was the Diuell of Edmonton, no such man, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: The Coniurer coosen'd him with a candles end, hee was an Asse.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: But there was one Smug, a Smith, would haue made a horse laugh, and broke his halter, as they say.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: O, but the poore man had got a shrewd mischance, one day.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: How, Gossip?

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: He had drest a Rogue Iade i'the morning, that had the Staggers, and had got such a spice of 'hem himselfe, by noone, as they would not away all the Play time, doe what hee could, for his heart.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: 'Twas his part, Gossip, he was to be drunke, by his part.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: Say you so, I vnderstood not so much.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTA.
prose: Would wee had such an other part, and such a man in this play, I feare 'twill be an excellent dull thing.

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: Expect, intend it.

plays.play_title: The second Intermeane after the second Act.

segments.head: The second Intermeane after the second Act.

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: Why, this is duller and duller! intolerable! scuruy! neither Diuel nor Foole in this Play! pray God, some on vs be not a witch, Gossip, to forespeake the matter thus.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: I feare we are all such, and we were old enough: But we are not all old enough to make one witch. How like you the Vice i'the Play.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: Which is he?

speeches.speaker: MIR.
prose: Three or foure: old Couetousnesse, the sordid Peny-boy, the Money-bawd, who is a flesh-bawd too, they say.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: But here is neuer a Fiend to carry him away. Besides, he has neuer a wooden dagger! I'ld not giue a rush for a Vice, that has not a wooden dagger to snap at euery body he meetes.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: That was the old way, Gossip, when Iniquity came in like Hokos Pokos, in a Iuglers ierkin, with false skirts. like the Knaue of Clubs! but now they are attir'd like men and women o' the time, the Vices, male and female! Prodigality like a young heyre, and his Mistresse Money (whose fauours he scatters like counters) prank't vp like a prime Lady, the Infanta of the Mines.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: I, therein they abuse an honorable Princesse, it is thought.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: By whom is it so thought? or where lies the abuse?

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: Plaine in the stiling her Infanta, and giuing her three names.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: Take heed, it lie not in the vice of your interpretation: what haue Aurelia, Clara, Pecunia to do with any person? do they any more, but expresse the property of Money, which is the daughter of earth, and drawne out of the Mines? Is there nothing to be call'd Infanta, but what is subiect to exception? Why not the Infanta of the Beggers? or Infanta o'the Gipsies? as well as King of Beggers, and King of Gipsies?

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: Well, and there were no wiser then I, I would sow him in a sack, and send him by sea to his Princesse.

speeches.speaker: MIRT.
prose: Faith, and hee heard you Censure, he would goe neere to sticke the Asses eares to your high dressing, and perhaps to all ours for harkening to you.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: By'r Lady but he should not to mine, I would harken, and harken, and censure, if I saw cause, for th'other Princesse sake Pokahontas, surnam'd the blessed, whom hee has abus'd indeed (and I doe censure him, and will censure him) to say she came foorth of a Tauerne, was said like a paltry Poet.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: That's but one Gossips opinion, and my Gossip Tatle's too! but what saies Expectation, here, she sits sullen and silent.

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Troth I expect their Office, their great Office! the Staple, what it will be! they haue talk't on't, but wee see't not open yet; would Butter would come in, and spread it-selfe a little to vs.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: Or the butter-box, Buz, the Emissary.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: When it is churn'd, and dish't, we shall heare of it.

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: If it be fresh and sweet butter; but say it be sower and wheyish.

speeches.speaker: MIR.
prose: Then it is worth nothing, meere pot-butter, fit to be spent in suppositories, or greasing coach-wheeles, stale stinking butter, and such I feare it is, by the being barrell'd vp so long.

speeches.speaker: EXPECTATION.
prose: Or ranke Irish butter.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: Haue patience Gossips, say that contrary to our expectations it proue right, seasonable, salt butter.

speeches.speaker: MIR.
prose: Or to the time of yeer, in Lent, delicate Almond butter! I haue a sweet tooth yet, and I will hope the best; and sit downe as quiet, and calme as butter; looke as smooth, and soft as butter; be merry, and melt like butter; laugh and be fat like butter: so butter answer my expectation, and be not mad butter; If it be: It shall both Iuly and December see. I say no more, But— Dixi.

plays.play_title: The third Intermeane after the third Act.

segments.head: The third Intermeane after the third Act.

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: A notable tough Rascall! this old Peny-boy! right City-bred!

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: In Siluer-streete, the Region of money, a good seat for a Vsurer.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: He has rich ingredients in him, I warrant you, if they were extracted, a true receit to make an Alderman, an' he were well wrought vpon, according to Art.

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: I would faine see an Alderman in chimia! that is a treatise of Aldermanity truely written.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: To shew how much it differs from Vrbanity.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: I, or humanity. Either would appeare in this Peny-boy, an' hee were rightly distill'd. But how like you the newes? you are gone from that.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: O, they are monstrous! scuruy! and stale! and too exotick! ill cook'd! and ill dish'd!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: They were as good, yet, as butter could make them!

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose:
In a word, they were beastly buttered! he shall neuer come o' my bread more, nor my in mouth, if I can helpe it. I haue had better newes from the bake-house, by ten thousand parts, in a morning: or the conduicts in Westminster! all the newes of Tutle-street, and both the Alm'ries! the two Sanctuaries
. long, and round Wool-staple! with Kings-street, and Chanon-row to boot!

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: I, my Gossip Tatle knew what fine slips grew in Gardiners-lane; who kist the Butchers wife with the Cowes-breath; what matches were made in the bowling-Alley, and what bettes wonne and lost; how much grieft went to the Mill and what besides: who coniur'd in Tutle-fields, and how many? when they neuer came there. And which Boy rode vpon Doctor Lambe, in the likenesse of a roaring Lyon, that runne away with him in his teeth, and ha's not deuour'd him yet.

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: Why, I had it from my maid Ioane Heare-say: and shee had it from a limbe o'the schoole, shee saies, a little limbe of nine yeere old; who told her, the Master left out his coniuring booke one day, and hee found it, and so the Fable came about. But whether it were true, or no, we Gossips are bound to beleeue it, an't be once out, and a foot: how should wee entertaine the time else, or finde our selues in fashionable discourse, for all companies, if we do not credit all, and make more of it, in the reporting?

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose:
For my part, I beleeue it: and there were no wiser then I, I would haue ne'er a cunning Schoole-Master in England. I meane a Cunning-Man, a Schoole-Master; that is a Coniurour, or a Poet, or that had any acquaintance with a Poet. They make all their schollers Play-boyes! Is't not a fine sight, to see all our children made Enterluders? Doe wee pay our money for this? wee send them to learne their

Grammar, and their Terence, and they learne their play-books? well, they talke, we shall haue no more Parliaments (God blesse vs) but an'wee haue, I hope, Zeale-of-the-land Buzy, and my Gossip, Rabby Trouble-truth will start vp, and see we shall haue painfull good Ministers to keepe Schoole, and Catechise our youth, and not teach 'hem to speake Playes, and Act Fables of false newes, in this manner, to the super-uexation of Towne and Countrey, with a wanion.

plays.play_title: The fourth Intermeane after the fourth Act.

segments.head: The fourth Intermeane after the fourth Act.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: Why? This was the worst of all! the Catastrophe!

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: The matter began to be good, but now: and he has spoyl'd it all, with his Begger there!

speeches.speaker: MIRT.
prose: A beggerly Iacke it is, I warrant him, and a kin to the Poet.

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: Like enough, for hee had the chiefest part in his play, if you marke it.

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Absurdity on him, for a huge ouergrowne Play-maker! why should he make him liue againe, when they, and we all thought him dead? If he had left him to his ragges, there had beene an end of him.

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: I, but set a beggar on horse-backe, hee'll neuer linne till hee be a gallop.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: The young heyre grew a fine Gentleman, in this last Act!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: So he did, Gossip: and kept the best company.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: And feasted 'hem, and his Mistresse!

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: And shew'd her to 'hem all! was not iealous!

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: But very communicatiue, and liberall, and beganne to be magnificent, if the churle his father would haue let him alone.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: It was spitefully done o' the Poet, to make the Chuffe take him off in his heighth, when he was going to doe all his braue deedes!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: To found an Academy!

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: Erect a Colledge!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Plant his Professors, and water his Lectures.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: With wine, gossips, as he meant to doe, and then to defraud his purposes?

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Kill the hopes of so many towardly young spirits?

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: As the Doctors?

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: And the Courtiers! I protest, I was in loue with Master Fitton. He did weare all he had, from the hat-band, to the shooe-tye, so politically, and would stoop, and leere?

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: And lie so, in waite for a piece of wit, like a Mouse-trap?

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Indeed Gossip, so would the little Doctor, all his behauiour was meere glister! O' my conscience, hee would make any parties physicke i' the world worke, with his discourse.

speeches.speaker: MIR.
prose: I wonder they would suffer it, a foolish old fornicating Father, to rauish away his sonnes Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: And all her women, at once, as hee did!

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: I would ha' flyen in his gypsies face i'faith.

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: It was a plaine piece of politicall incest, and worthy to be brought afore the high Commission of wit. Suppose we were to censure him, you are the youngest voyce, Gossip Tatle, beginne.

speeches.speaker: TATLE.
prose: Mary, I would ha' the old conicatcher coozen'd of all he has, i'the young heyres defence, by his learn'd Counsell, Mr Picklocke!

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: I would rather the Courtier had found out some tricke to begge him, from his estate!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Or the Captaine had courage enough to beat him.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: Or the fine Madrigall-man, in rime, to haue runne him out o' the Countrey, like an Irish rat.

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: No, I would haue Master Pyed-mantle, her Graces Herald, to pluck downe his hatchments, reuerse his coat-armour, and nullifie him for no Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Nay, then let Master Doctor dissect him, haue him open'd, and his tripes translated to Lickfinger, to make a probation dish of.

speeches.speaker: CEN. TAT.
prose: Agreed! Agreed!

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: Faith I would haue him flat disinherited, by a decree of Court, bound to make restitution of the Lady Pecunia, and the vse of her body to his sonne.

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: And her traine, to the Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: And both the Poet, and himselfe, to aske them all forgiuenesse!

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: And vs too.

speeches.speaker: CEN.
verse: In two large sheetes of paper—

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Or to stand in a skin of parchment, (which the Court please)

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: And those fill'd with newes!

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: And dedicated to the sustaining of the Staple!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Which their Poet hath let fall, most abruptly?

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: Banckruptly, indeede!

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: You say wittily, Gossip, and therefore let a protest goe out against him.

speeches.speaker: MIR.
prose: A mourniuall of protests; or a gleeke at least!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: In all our names:

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: For a decay'd wit—

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Broken—

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: Non-soluent—

speeches.speaker: CENSVRE.
prose: And, for euer, forfet—

speeches.speaker: MIRTH.
prose: To scorne, of Mirth?

speeches.speaker: CEN.
prose: Censure!

speeches.speaker: EXP.
prose: Expectation!

speeches.speaker: TAT.
prose: Subsign'd. Tatle, Stay, they come againe.
